Deploy DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GPU Cloud for 1M-Context Inference

 Fareed Khan 

Updated on 21 Oct 2026

# Deploy DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GPU Cloud for 1M-Context Inference

TABLE OF CONTENTS

### Key Takeaways

- DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 552B backbone parameters, 8B active per prompt token and 16B per generated token, and a 1,048,576-token context.
- Its global KV cache is 890 bytes per token, so a full one-million-token prompt needs under 1 GB of global KV.
- A DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash deployment fits on one 8x NVIDIA H100 machine once the Engram tables and their scales, about 189 GiB, move to pinned host memory, leaving about 36 GiB of resident weights on each card.
- vLLM 0.31.0 serves it with tensor parallel 8, a 4,096-token batch budget and 0.92 memory utilisation, the NVIDIA H100 configuration from the vLLM recipe.
- The endpoint serves thinking with a 1 to 100 effort setting, OpenAI-format tool calls and image input, and Claude Code can drive it directly.
- The whole deployment runs on one machine at $20.80 per hour on demand, or from $14.56 per hour reserved, billed per minute.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is an updated release of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 552 billion backbone parameters that reads text and images, writes text and holds up to 1,048,576 tokens of context. Only 8 billion parameters are active for each prompt token and 16 billion for each generated token. The whole checkpoint is 510 GB, and once its Engram memory moves to host RAM, a DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash deployment fits on one node of eight 80 GB GPUs.

This guide deploys it on a single Hyperstack virtual machine with 8x NVIDIA H100-80G-PCIe-NVLink GPUs, using vLLM 0.31.0 and the NVIDIA H100 configuration from the vLLM recipe for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: tensor parallel 8, the Engram tables in pinned host memory, a 4,096-token batch budget and the full one-million-token context. The result is a private, OpenAI-compatible endpoint with thinking, a reasoning effort setting from 1 to 100, tool calling and image input, ready for an agent harness such as Claude Code.

Most of what lets the model fit on one machine comes from its design rather than from tuning. DeepSeek puts its global KV cache at 890 bytes per token, about a quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash's, and 196 billion of its parameters are Engram lookup tables that are read rather than computed, so they can sit in host memory. If you have followed our DeepSeek-V4-Pro multi-node Kubernetes guide, this is the opposite shape: one virtual machine, no cluster and no orchestration layer.

## Inside DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: 552B Parameters, 8B Active in Prefill

DeepSeek titles the release Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression, and almost every component serves that aim.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at a glance

Six numbers that shape the deployment.

BACKBONE

552B parameters

Mixture of experts: 1 shared and 384 routed experts, 6 routed active per token

ACTIVE PER TOKEN

8B prefill, 16B decode

A causal encoder-decoder lets most prompt tokens skip the decoder

CONTEXT

1,048,576 tokens

YaRN scaling, factor 16, from a 65,536-token original window

GLOBAL KV CACHE

890 bytes per token

About a quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash's, stored in FP4

ENGRAM MEMORY

196B parameters

Two n-gram lookup tables, at layers 1 and 14

CHECKPOINT

510.3 GB, 48 shards

MXFP4 experts, FP8 dense weights, MIT licence

Sources: the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash model cards, the technical report, config.json and the 1017 repository file list.

### The 1017 Weights: Same Architecture, Stronger Scores

DeepSeek describes DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 as a minor update to the launch release. The vLLM recipe records that its config.json, tokenizer files and prompt encoding match the launch repository byte for byte, and that the index holds the same 96,085 tensors, so only the weights change and one command serves either checkpoint.

The gains are broad. Terminal-Bench 4.0 rises from 31.2 to 42.3 and HLE without tools from 36.8 to 42.6, and DeepSeek reports shorter outputs and task execution times.

From the launch weights to 1017

Every benchmark on the 1017 model card moves up. Rows are sorted by the size of the gain; the hollow dot is the launch checkpoint, the filled dot the 1017 weights.

Launch weights 1017 weights

Chart: scores for the launch weights and the 1017 weights on eleven benchmarks. Terminal-Bench 4.0 rises from 31.2 to 42.3, ProgramBench from 20.3 to 29.1, Apex Bench from 64.6 to 72.1 and HLE without tools from 36.8 to 42.6; every row improves.

Source: the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 model card. Terminal-Bench 4.0 uses the Claude Code harness and DeepSWE v1.1 the Mini-SWE-V2 harness, as the card states.

### A Causal Encoder-Decoder That Nearly Halves Prefill

The 40 transformer layers are split into a 20-layer causal encoder and a 20-layer decoder. In a decoder-only model, every layer derives its keys and values from its own hidden states, so every prompt token must run through all 40 layers. Here the decoder global KV cache is projected from the final encoder hidden state instead, which lets most prompt tokens stop at the end of the encoder.

According to the technical report, this nearly halves prefill computation, and it is where the 8 billion and 16 billion figures come from: a prompt token runs the encoder, a generated token runs both halves. DeepSeek designed the split for agentic work, which the report describes as increasingly input-heavy, with frequent tool calls generating long prefills.

How far a token travels

Most prompt tokens stop at the encoder. Generated tokens run all 40 layers.

Drawn from section 2.2 of the technical report. The decoder still keeps a 128-token sliding window, so the last 128 prompt tokens also pass through it, a step DeepSeek calls Decoder SWA Bounded Replay.

### Compressed Sparse Attention 2: Forty Layers, Four Global Caches

From layer 2 onwards, every layer combines a 128-token sliding window with a sparse view of the global context further back; layers 0 and 1 use the sliding window alone. Compressed Sparse Attention 2, or CSA2, decides where that global context comes from by giving each of those 38 layers one of three static modes:

- Full layers compute their own global KV, score it with a lightweight indexer and keep the top 512 entries for each query.
- Reindex layers reuse the global KV of the latest Full layer, but score it with their own indexer query and pick a fresh top 512.
- Reuse layers take both the KV and the top 512 selection from an earlier layer and run attention directly.

Only four of the 40 layers compute a global cache at all: layers 2, 8, 14 and 20. The encoder stores one global entry for every two tokens, while the decoder keeps one per token. In the decoder, layer 20 also builds a candidate pool of 2,048 blocks of eight positions, and the four Reindex layers search only those 16,384 candidates, so their cost per query stays constant however long the context grows.

Forty layers, four global caches

Each square is one layer, coloured by how it obtains its global context.

Layer modes from section 4.2.1 of the technical report and the kv_source_layer_ids, index_source_layer_ids and compress_ratios fields in config.json.

### 890 Bytes of Global KV per Token

The saving has two sources. One is sharing caches across layers; the other is precision: DeepSeek trains the main KV cache to be stored in FP4, as E2M1 values with one E4M3 scale per 16 channels, while the sliding-window cache stays in FP8. Together they put the global KV footprint at 890 bytes per token, 3.9 times smaller than DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the model in our DeepSeek-V4 deployment guide, and 437 times smaller than DeepSeek-V1.

Global KV cache per token across DeepSeek generations

Bytes per token on a logarithmic scale. Each generation cuts the footprint by a large factor.
